segments.text: There’s never been as big a shock to the semiconductor industry
as the current surge in demand from AI. AI is driving incredible computing demand.
Easily 40-50% above our maximum capacity, which I’ve never seen before.
Progress in AI has been driven by exponentially increasing compute.
To sustain that progress, foundries like Intel will need to manufacture far more
leading-edge compute, both by producing more chips and by improving what each chip can do.
But the production of these chips is bottlenecked by tools that Intel buys from their suppliers.
Most famously, ASML’s EUV machines. If they don’t have the equipment,
they can’t make the chips here. I spent two days touring Intel’s fabs to
prepare for these interviews with its leadership. I wanted to understand what it takes to
manufacture the world’s most advanced chips and how hardware is shaping the future of AI.
I’m joined by Chris Auth, who leads development of all the processes
that are currently under manufacturing. The thing I want to understand in more
concrete detail is how the development of a new process actually happens.
If 14A is going to come out in three years or two years from now,
what is happening from now till then? I want you to walk me through as much
detail as you can, everything from the level of “how is the yield improving?” to what
kind of telemetry you guys look at? What kind of experiments do you guys run?
I want to understand what is going to happen over the next two years as concretely as possible.
14A has been in development for about three-plus years at this stage,
so quite a bit of pre-work has been done to get it to the stage that it’s at right now.
Right now, we’re getting very close to where we’re finalizing the process.
We’re finalizing the tool sets that it will be manufactured on,
and we’re working on the fine-tuning of each of the process steps.
There are about 2,000 steps in the factory that you have to go do.
You need to do really intricate work at each one of those to make sure it’s fine-tuned,
it can go into manufacturing, it can run thousands of wafers a week on this process,
and it can be repeatable every single time. Right now, you might have a certain yield.
Walk me through how that increases month over month.
There’s a line running at 14A. What happens from now till next
month that will result in the yield changing? How do you identify where the defects are?
How do you fix that? There’s a constant
process that we go through in identifying defects. There are two main ways that we’ll identify them.
One is we have inline metrology. We have tools that will look at
the wafers and say, “Ah, there’s a defect there, there’s a defect there, there’s a defect there.”
Then also at the end of line, either electrical test or we sort and see where the fails are.
We will identify failures, and then we will get analysis on those failures.
We’ll cross-section it. You were in the TEM lab yesterday,
and you saw how you can get cross-sections. You’ll get a cross-section of a defect,
and from that, you’ll be able to say, “Oh, that defect is between these layers, so it
must have come from this section of the flow. Oh, we have inline metrology in that section,
which has identified defects. Those are the defects we need to go after.”
What we’ve learned is that you don’t want to do too much innovation in one node,
because the more innovation that you do, the more complex it becomes.
While you’ll be able to get that to work, you need to hit a certain schedule, and that’s the
schedule that your customer ultimately wants. Having that predictable schedule is a key piece.
You’ve got to figure out how much innovation you can put in in order to meet the customer’s
requirements in the timeline that they need it. Intel learned how costly that tradeoff can
be with delays to its 10 nanometer node, whose original target launch date was 2016,
but which didn’t begin manufacturing until 2018. Usually Intel has been the keeper of Moore’s Law,
a new cadence of manufacturing every two years, but their last
set of products slipped almost four years. Intel today having its worst day in four months,
the stock now down more than 15%. I also want to point out Taiwan
Semiconductor up 13% off of Intel’s bad news. Walk me through what lessons you think Intel
has learned from 10 nanometer. Ten nanometer was a good example
of where we had very aggressive targets. We were doing what was called hyperscaling
at the time, so we were scaling much faster than what had been historically done.
In order to do that, we came up with all sorts of innovative ideas on how we could achieve that
without new tools, because the tools weren’t ready.
That put a lot of burden on the process and a lot of burden on the engineers.
Now, at the end of the day, 10 nanometer is a great technology.
It has world-class yield, it has world-class performance, it has world-class cost,
but it took us longer to do that than what we would have liked.
So we’ve tried to take that learning into future technology nodes and say, “Hey, we
need to limit the amount of innovation we put in there to make sure that we keep it on schedule.”
What do you think was the main technology that should’ve been saved for a future version?
EUV was probably the big thing. When we started to define 10 nanometer,
the conclusion was EUV was not ready. EUV is extreme ultraviolet lithography.
It prints chip patterns with light at a wavelength of 13.5 nanometers,
about 14 times shorter than that emitted by previous tools that chipmakers had relied on.
The shorter the wavelength, the finer the features that a single exposure can print.
But Intel decided this technology wasn’t going to be ready in time.
TSMC transitioned to EUV much sooner.
It put EUV into volume manufacturing in 2019 and ramped it up further on its 5nm node in 2020.
Intel’s first EUV process did not reach products until 2023, so TSMC had about four more years
of experience with these machines. Yesterday, we were at the research
lab getting a preview of 2D materials and CFET and ruthenium interconnects.
I’m curious about how you decide whether that technology is mature enough for the next node.
One thing that did also come out of 10 nanometer is we started to define a set of maturity metrics.
We use those maturity metrics in a process which we call phase gate, where we would say,
“To go from pathfinding into development, these are the criteria that we need to go hit.”
There are yield criteria, defect criteria, performance criteria, and we need to hit those
in order to move to the next set of the flow. If there’s something that doesn’t make that,
then it misses that, and it goes on to the next technology.
We focus on the items that are ready and we can run and put into a process, because
one of the key things is staying on schedule. Staying on schedule is hard partly because new
transistor designs take decades to mature. Modern chip transistors evolved from the
planar MOS transistor, demonstrated in 1960. The history of transistors since has been
the progression from two dimensions into three. Each development that Chris goes on to describe,
from FinFET to gate-all-around, is a step in that progression.
So it’ll help to first look at a basic transistor and how its parts have changed over time.
A transistor is basically a switch. When it’s turned on, it allows current
to flow between its two ends, which are called the source and the drain.
A piece called a gate sits on top of the silicon between the source and the drain.
Applying a positive voltage to the gate turns the switch on, because the positive
voltage pulls negatively charged electrons in the silicon beneath up toward the gate.
However, a thin layer of insulation stops them from actually reaching the gate.
So the electrons collect just beneath that insulation and form a thin conducting path
from the source to the drain. This is called the channel.
Remove the voltage and the electrons disperse, the channel disappears, and the switch turns off.
As transistors shrank, the source and the drain got so close together
that current could flow through the channel even when the switch was supposed to be off.
We needed a better way to control the channel and prevent current from leaking through.
The fix was to give the gate a tighter grip on the channel by touching it from more sides.
In the original planar transistor, the gate only touches the channel from the top.
The FinFET transistor squeezes the channel into a thin vertical fin of silicon.
The gate drapes over the fin, so it controls the channel from three sides.
The next progression from there was to cover not only the top and
the sides of the channel, but also the bottom. This technology is called gate-all-around, and
it slices the channel into thin ribbons, each of which gets completely wrapped around by the gate.
But getting gate-all-around to work required new materials and new manufacturing steps.
To build these floating ribbons of silicon, you first sandwich them between alternating
layers of a temporary placeholder material, which holds the space where the gate will eventually go.
We use a placeholder because the materials in the real gate wouldn’t survive the processing
that comes after, which involves baking the wafer at around 1,000 degrees Celsius.
Once these hot steps are done, chipmakers etch away the
placeholder, leaving the ribbons suspended. Then they fill the gaps around every ribbon
with a thin coat of a special insulator called a high-k material, whose purpose is to let the gate
pull more strongly on the channel. And then on top of this material,
they put the metal of the gate itself. FinFET was demonstrated in a lab in 1989
and reached volume production at Intel in 2011. A gate-all-around transistor had been demonstrated
a year earlier, in 1988, but Samsung didn’t begin producing gate-all-around chips until 2022.
So these ideas, FinFET and gate-all-around, were developed around the same time,
but they reached production a decade apart. I wanted to ask Chris why it took so long to
get to this current gate-all-around technology. Maybe you can walk me through the process of
getting into high-volume manufacturing. I want to understand concretely,
once you have an idea that, “Hey, we’re going to make the channel smaller, we’re going to
surround it…” All the other problems of material science, figuring out how to not destroy the gate,
how do they actually get figured out? Why does it take so long?
Gate-all-around’s a good example, because back in the ’90s we knew of this idea.
But we knew there were going to be these problems on how you put this
into high-volume manufacturing. At the same time, there are other
things like high-K metal gate. There’s strained silicon,
there’s FinFETs that are out there. It’s a question of when’s the right
time to go and tackle those? Well, you don’t want to
tackle something before you have to. If you have these other things that can drive
performance, you would go and do that. So we went through this path.
We did strained silicon, high-K metal gate, we did FinFETs, and then it became, “Well,
we need to do things further. How do we get there?”
Well, gate-all-around’s really the ultimate transistor out there.
Maybe it’s time to go and start tackling some of those issues that you have.
You’re right, now you have to look at how do you put high-K metal gate in with gate-all-around.
It’s that innovation that takes time. Sometimes you need new materials.
Sometimes you need a different tool in order to be able to do some of the
things that you need to go do, and that requires invention from the tool vendors.
You have to go to the tool vendor and say, “Hey, I need a tool that can do XYZ.
I need a gas that can deposit this particular material that goes into that.
I need a heating chuck that has this characteristic to it.”
All those things take time. Some of it’s iterative,
where you have to run a gate-all-around transistor and say, “Oh, well, that didn’t work.
Let me figure out what was wrong with my hypothesis and
try it again with some different structure.” How has the nature of R&D changed from the era of
just making planar transistors smaller and smaller and getting the benefits of Dennard scaling,
to the world we’re in today? Is it just a totally different
kind of R&D process? Previously it was,
“Let’s make things smaller, smaller, smaller.” Now you look at all these other facets
of performance at the same time, and improvements in size don’t come as easily.
Walk me through whether there was some crucial change in the R&D process at that point.
If you look at the ’80s and ’90s, yes, it was driven really by Dennard scaling, lithography.
We just made things smaller, transistors got faster, they got more reliable,
and it was a very predictable cadence. When we started to hit the 2000s, we saw,
“That’s not good enough anymore. We need to do something different.”
To me, it became this golden age of innovation. For each technology node,
how are you going to provide more scaling? How are you going to provide more performance?
It drove things like strained silicon. It drove high-K metal gate.
It drove FinFETs. It drove gate-all-around. It drove backside power.
These are things that in the ’80s and ’90s you would be like, “Oh no,
we’re not touching any of that,” because we just continued to have the same process flow.
We just scaled it, scaled it, scaled it. But for somebody like me who’s a
transistor junkie, it’s awesome, because now the playbook’s open.
You can do all sorts of things out there. You can bring in new materials.
Just look at the number of materials we used to use in the ’90s versus the materials today.
It’s probably gone up 10X. There’s a lot of innovation.
There’s atomic layer deposition. You’re controlling this stuff atom by atom.
So it’s changed a lot how you approach the process.
Before, it was, “Try to not change anything.” Now it’s, “Take the sledgehammer and start tearing
the thing up and come up with some new idea.” For 14A, Intel is using a new kind
of lithography machine: High-NA EUV. It uses the same extreme ultraviolet light
as today’s EUV machines, but changes the optics. NA, or numerical aperture, is a measure of how
wide a cone of light the machine’s mirrors can focus onto the wafer.
The wider the cone you can focus, the smaller the spot that your light can carve.
Standard EUV machines have an NA of 0.33. High-NA widens it to 0.55.
So High-NA can print features about 1.7 times smaller in a single pass.
When features are smaller than the lithography machine can print, chipmakers have to split
the pattern across several passes, each printing a different set of features.
The most tightly packed patterns can require two, three, or even four passes.
Each additional pass takes up valuable time on a machine that costs around $200 million,
and it introduces another opportunity for defects. High-NA machines cost about twice as much,
but they can reduce the number of passes that are needed.
So the question which determines whether they justify their higher
price is how much more time they save and how much they reduce the risk of defects.
Now you guys are using High-NA EUV tools for 14A, whereas TSMC has said
that they don’t make economic sense yet for them. How do you decide whether the next litho tool is
the one that is ready to adopt or not? High-NA’s a good example of where,
because of the architecture of our technology versus TSMC’s, we make different conclusions
off of the same tool set. We use backside power.
That means that you actually alleviate some of the pitch requirements you have on the front side.
That allows you to print that directly with High-NA.
TSMC has to run tighter pitches because they don’t have backside power,
and they can’t do that with High-NA, so they have to use double patterning EUV.
So for them, it’s not very helpful. For us, it is very helpful.
Now at 14A, we’ve left it as an option, and it’s something that we’ll have a discussion
with the customer on, because there’s some value proposition to it, and there’s some
complexity that it adds. Chris is referring to
a feature called backside power. A chip has two different kinds of wiring.
Power lines deliver electricity to the transistors, and they need to be thick.
Signal lines let the transistors talk to each other.
They’re much thinner, but they need to be spaced apart so that the signal from one wire doesn’t
interfere with the signal from another. In the past, all of these power lines
and signal lines had to be crammed together on top of the transistors.
Intel’s newest process moves these power lines below the transistors, to the back of the wafer.
This frees up space on top, so the signal lines don’t have to be packed as tightly.
This change makes High-NA worth it for Intel. Without backside power, the wiring is so
tight that it would require multiple passes to print, even with High-NA.
With backside power, a single High-NA pass is enough.
Outside companies can now commission Intel to manufacture chips that they’ve designed.
They follow Intel’s process design kit, or PDK: the menu of what a given process can build,
and the rules for building it. Do you need to lock that into
your PDK right now for customers who are planning on developing on 14A?
It’s an option in the PDK today, and we’re handling it as a customer-by-customer
discussion as to whether or not they want to go down that path or not.
For 18A, there was public reporting that there were delays in or issues with the PDK,
such that some instructions didn’t work, and it was difficult for people to use
your foundry to build their chips. Tell me about the process of Intel
becoming a foundry and then having a PDK that other customers can use to make
whatever chip they’re making as well. There’s definitely a learning curve to
how you become a foundry. That’s something that our
competitors have gone through as well. PDK is a good example of that.
For decades, we’ve been an IDM. We’ve gone to our product teams
and shown them our transistor data, and we share that data back and forth, and we haven’t
had a formal PDK-type process. So that’s a new process that
we’ve had to implement on 18A. 18A started out not having a PDK.
There’s definitely a lot of feedback we’ve gotten from the customers as to what they expect
for quality and maturity of the PDK and what sort of information they want to see in there.
We’ve tried to incorporate that into making sure that we have a PDK that
meets our customers’ requirements. That’s where we’ve ended up.
We’re starting to get PDKs that have this, and 14A will have that from the get-go.
It has very high quality PDKs. Again, there are maturity metrics for
what is a PDK 0.5 versus a 0.9 versus a 1.0. We’re constantly going through and taking
customer feedback and incorporating that into the quality of our PDK.
For most of its history, Intel’s fabs made only Intel’s chips.
That could be part of what allowed TSMC to gain an edge.
Serving many customers gave TSMC more wafers to learn from, more revenue to reinvest,
and more pressure to hit deadlines. Basically, all enterprise customers
have a shared set of product requirements that you have to meet if you want to even
start talking about doing business with them. These are things like SSO, so employees can
log into your app with their company accounts, or directory sync, so that whenever someone leaves,
their access gets shut off automatically. These features are harder to get right than
you think, and the risk-reward for building them in-house doesn’t really make sense:
a slightly better version of SSO probably won’t accelerate your growth,
but a broken one will definitely stunt it. WorkOS gives you access to battle-tested versions
of all the most common enterprise features—things like SSO, SCIM, RBAC, audit logs, and more.
WorkOS also has versions of these features that are purpose-built for agents, so they can log in,
grab the right permissions, and take actions within your product.
All of these features can be plugged in with just a few lines of code, so you can
add them and get started selling to enterprises. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Thinking Machines—as well
as more than 3,000 other companies—all rely on WorkOS to meet their enterprise requirements.
If you want to join them, go to workos.com and tell them that I sent you.
If a butterfly flapped its wings in the ’60s, could you imagine a world where gate-all-around
is not even a word people have heard of, an idea people are familiar with, but people are thinking
of an extremely different branch of the tech tree? How far down the tech tree do you think
things could be totally different? Could it be that we’re not even using copper?
If you look at, say, transistors and interconnects, where we’ve gotten to,
as far as the transistor and gate-all-around and it being the ideal transistor structure,
was somewhat inevitable. As I said, in the ’90s we were
already talking about these types of things. Backside power, that one’s pretty out there.
Even in the ’90s, the idea that you’re going to strip off the entire silicon substrate and put
lines on the backside, that one is probably something that’s a little bit out there.
Copper, of course copper wires are the best, so I don’t know how you would end
up somewhere else besides copper. But you guys are exploring other—
For some of the very tightest pitches, it’s inevitable that you will replace copper.
That’s a good example of where you will have another material that will come in there.
But for the larger lines, I think copper is about where it’s at.
Once you start to do gate-all-around transistors and you do backside power,
now you start to enter a very different regime.
Now you see it’s not, “Hey, there’s just some substrate and you stack everything on top.”
Now you’ve got a transistor which is floating in interconnect, and you’re like, “Okay, well,
why don’t I have transistors, interconnect, a little more transistors, more interconnect?”
This whole 3D stacking that we now do with just discrete chips that we stack on top of each other.
Now you’re like, “Why can’t I just build an entire structure like this?”
You see it with memory, NAND, DRAM. They have some incredible 3D structures.
NAND already does it, DRAM talks about it, but I think that DRAM inevitably
is going to go there too. A lot of people say, “Oh no,
we’re not going to do this because we can’t do it in the next five years.”
Well, come on, let’s put a larger timescale on this.
Let’s put 10 years, 20 years. In 2045, do you think you could do it?
Now you start to say, “Oh yeah, I could see us having some pretty
exotic structures at that point.” We limit ourselves by what we see
as possible in the next four years. As I’ve always said, when people say,
“How do you see technology scaling going?”, we have visibility for about four years.
Then you get out to the four years, and you go, “Yeah, I think there’s something
we can do another four years out of that.” And you get to that four years, and you’re like,
“Yeah, I think you can do something.” But if you start to talk about 10 years,
it becomes hard to say what it’s going to be. Chris’s idea of building upward could start
with the transistors themselves. Chips use two types of transistor,
called n-type and p-type, which work the same way, but with the charges reversed.
Nearly every circuit is built by pairing them up. Today, chipmakers build them side by side.
The next step is to stack them directly on top of each other in order to save space.
In principle, that fits twice as many transistors into the same area.
This design is called a CFET, short for complementary field-effect transistor.
But every extra layer adds manufacturing steps and cost, and also leads to heat building
up that doesn’t have a clear way to escape. Because logic consumes more power than memory, you
can’t do stacks of DRAM that make HBM or 3D NAND as easily with logic, because of the heat issue.
Is that the fundamental issue over the long run? How you—
Thermals. There are three things you have when you try to say, “Hey, what limits compute?”
It’s how fast can you do the switch, so the frequency of the device.
How much power does it take in order to do that switch, so the power efficiency of it.
The third one is, how do you dissipate the heat that was generated by doing that switch?
That’s the thermals piece of it. These are not new problems.
You can go back 20 years and you can see articles on these three things.
The question is, thermals… how do you deal with that, particularly when you
start to talk about these 3D-type devices? There is a need for that sort of system-level
analysis and simulation tools. I think we’re in its infancy
because we’ve just started to look at this. It is a limiter, and it will be a limiter, but
again, these are problems that we can go solve. The problems respond to work, but engineering time
is finite, and so are the wafers for experiments. Deciding where they go across thousands
of problems is itself one of the hardest parts of bringing up a node.
I sat in on one of Intel’s Hot Topics meetings, where those decisions get made.
I’m here with Kevin Fischer, who was laying down the law this morning at the Hot Topics meeting,
where you guys were discussing how you’re improving 18A and 18A-P technologies.
People would come to you with different experiments they were running,
different ideas they had for improving yield and performance, and then you and
your integration engineers would tell them what data you needed, how they should proceed,
how you think they could move things faster. I want people to have a sense of
the culture at these meetings. One thing I found striking is that this
is bottlenecking your most advanced node. You want progress to happen fast,
so you kind of lay down the hammer. I would say the average engineer doesn’t
understand the stakes or the urgency of how this is going to impact Intel’s bottom line,
how it’s going to impact our customer. They just have no visibility into those issues.
They will typically have a certain set of criteria that they want to go capture.
They’ll hit boundaries of, “I asked for something and someone said no, and I’m done.
I guess I can’t have this thing that I asked for.” One thing you learn in this industry is that
you will never have a complete data set. If you want to wait for a complete data set,
you’ve waited too long. It’s already too late.
A lot of what I end up doing in those meetings is deciding how much risk we’re
going to take on a certain decision or not take on a certain decision.
You need to say, “Look, do we go now? Do we start risking production?”
Because you’re risking the bottom line. You’re risking revenue.
I’m worried you’re going to put me in the light of being an ogre because I’m
putting the hammer down on people. That’s a great reputation to have.
It’s really conveying urgency. Every day counts.
Can you walk me through a particular issue that might come up?
One of the examples you saw this morning is epi nodules.
Epi is short for epitaxy, which means growing new material on top of an existing one.
Chipmakers flow gases over a heated wafer, and the gases leave atoms on its surface.
The crystal structure of the material underneath acts as a template.
Each new atom lines up with the atoms below it, and the new layer continues the same crystal.
Chipmakers use epitaxy at several stages of making a chip.
In the step Kevin describes, they use it to grow the source and the drain as small
crystals on either side of the gate. During the deposition of our epitaxy,
we get abnormal growth, a little thing like a tumor.
It’s growing super fast. That causes problems,
because one epi will short to the wrong epi and you get transistors not working.
Then you’ve got to narrow it down to how you’re going to fix it.
For the past decade, Intel’s chips have had this feature called Processor Trace.
When you turn it on, it starts recording all the code your program runs, and it captures
enough detail that you can go back later and reconstruct every single function call.
Most companies don’t need that level of detail. But Jane Street does: they need to investigate
specific, fleeting moments in their trading systems—things like
a delayed response to a network packet. Those events tend to be too brief for
most debugging tools to catch. So when one of Jane Street’s
engineers noticed Processor Trace, he started playing around with it.
And then he and a summer intern turned that exploration into a new tool called magic-trace.
Magic-trace leverages the output from Processor Trace to give Jane Street a
history of every function call leading up to a specific moment of interest.
This project was completely bottom-up—it started just as something that one
engineer thought would be valuable. And now, traders and developers across
Jane Street use magic-trace every single day. If you want to work somewhere where you’re trusted
to pursue the ideas that you think matter most, Jane Street is hiring researchers and engineers.
Go to janestreet.com/dwarkesh to learn more. One of the pieces that you observed this morning
was a special clean that we were looking at, which would eliminate the nodule.
The nodule would deposit, and then we’d get rid of it.
Some of the other discussion was about the source of the nodule.
Get rid of the source of the nodule. There’s some issue. How do you
decide what the source of it is? For the most part, we work highly parallel.
How do you decide? It’s not always evident
what the easiest way to fix the problem is, so you work on all the potential fixes.
Sometimes it’s not the one you expect first. Once we’ve identified it as a primary problem
for the technology, that’s where this Hot Topics meeting gets involved.
That’s how we align the resources into those engineering teams so that
we can accelerate the work. You said that there’s some
fast-track process where wafers can move through faster if they’re bottlenecking some experiment.
We have a tiered system of what we call hot boxes in the factory.
Every grade of hot box goes a little bit faster. It’s just how the factory prioritizes that
particular lot, that block of silicon that’s running through the factory.
Our highest grade of hot box, HotBox 1, races through the factory.
It gets priority at every single tool, but it’s a drag on the entire factory.
If you had a factory person in here, they don’t like playing that card,
because you end up using the tools inefficiently so that you can go super fast.
Think of it as a highway, and you set aside that one lane for the carpool,
which everyone could use, but you’re saying, “Okay, it’s just the carpool.”
That’s our HotBox 1. Everyone clear out of
that lane except for that one experiment, and that one experiment races down the highway.
Kevin’s job is deciding what goes onto the production line now, but the day before, I
went to Intel’s research lab with Jack Kavalieros to see ideas that aren’t ready for the node yet.
We started with wiring. A transistor is only useful once it’s connected
to others, and on a modern chip that takes more than a dozen layers of metal wire stacked
above the transistors, called interconnect. Those wires are made of copper, and as they
shrink, copper starts to run into trouble. Intel is exploring a replacement: ruthenium.
Ruthenium has higher resistivity, so why are you guys exploring ruthenium for the future?
Interestingly enough, as you scale the dimensions of those copper wires, you run into challenges.
For example, copper typically requires a liner in order to deposit the copper to fill those lines.
Ruthenium is very different in that regard because it’s a material that we can actually etch.
As such, by etching it, we don’t need that liner. Now you scale those very fine dimensions,
and if you can trade off that resistive liner with no liner, ruthenium starts to win.
There is a crossover point where ruthenium will have much better
conductivity, better resistivity than copper. That’s roughly in the 20-nanometer pitch range,
which means, if you can imagine, half of the pitch is your metal line, and the other half is
the dielectric that isolates them. So what is the liner?
Think of it almost like a glue layer or transition layer that we need in order to deposit the copper

Stacking transistors is still in the research lab. Stacking whole chips is already in production,
and it tackles a different problem: how separate chips communicate with each other.
Modern computers are divided into multiple parts, each optimized for a different task.
For example, Nvidia’s Blackwell data-center GPU joins two huge processor chips and surrounds them
with eight stacks of high-bandwidth memory. These chips have to constantly send
data back and forth with each other. And in AI, the speed of that traffic,
not the raw computation itself, is often what limits how fast the workload finishes.
Imagine two chips side by side, communicating through their facing edges.
If you double each chip’s width and length, you’ll have four times the area for circuitry,
but only twice the edge length for connections. This is the area-versus-perimeter problem.
As transistors become denser, a chip’s ability to do computations increases
faster than its ability to move data around. The industry has known about this problem
for years, so multiple technologies have been invented to address it.
The completed circuits must undergo two last operations: bonding and packaging.
Once a chip is made, it still has to be connected to other chips and to the rest of the computer.
That step is called packaging, and it has changed a lot in the last few decades.
At a high level, you can think of the evolution of packaging like this: initially,
chips were laid out side by side. Wires connecting them went out
the side of one chip to another. To allow for more communication
density, the industry introduced a shared piece of silicon, called an
interposer, for multiple chips to sit on. A chip can talk to other chips through the
wiring that runs directly through the interposer. This type of packaging is often called “2.5D”.
Another way to increase connection density is to bond chips directly to one another.
This allows for shorter connections between chips, but the early versions of this idea used solder
bumps, which are bulky and increased resistance. It would be better to skip the solder and fuse
the signal wire connections of the two chips directly to each other.
This is called hybrid bonding, and it is one of the technologies the
semiconductor industry is investing in the most. Hybrid bonding works by aligning the copper
interconnects of one chip with those of another. Then these chips are pushed together and heated
so their interconnects expand and bridge the gap between the chips.
This process makes the insulating surfaces around the copper bond as well.
And so by removing the solder bumps, you end up with much denser connections.
But the reason this technology is only now entering volume manufacturing is because
it took a while to iron out the alignment and defect challenges that it introduced.
In the packaging lab, I asked Tyler Osborn, a director in Intel’s advanced packaging
technology development group, how they put this into practice.
Intel has spent over 50 years optimizing its CPUs for speed.
But lots of these optimizations—like caching and branch prediction and
speculative execution—reduce predictability. The exact same instructions can take four
cycles to execute one time and 300 the next. When you stack billions of instructions together
and execute them across multiple threads and cores, these non-determinisms compound into
all sorts of hard-to-reproduce bugs. If you work on serious systems,
you’ve definitely experienced this. Antithesis solved this by doing something a bit
crazy: they built a 100% deterministic computer. They identified every single door in Intel’s x86
architecture where non-determinism could leak in—network packets, disk reads,
temperature sensors, even time itself. And they either welded each of these
shut or slotted in a controlled simulation. This deterministic computer is just a foundation.
On top of it, Antithesis built a testing platform that compresses
years of production hardening into minutes. It runs your software through thousands of
parallel worlds, injecting faults and intelligently steering each one
towards a one-in-a-billion failure that you’d never be able to test yourself.
This determinism is what’s behind all the other insane Antithesis features that I’ve
mentioned over the past few episodes. It’s what lets you reproduce any bug
and time travel to any point in the test run. Most importantly, it’s what lets you—or your
agents—trace every failure back to its root cause. Go to antithesis.com/dwarkesh to learn more.

we typically call wafer to wafer. We actually take a full wafer and
another wafer and bond them together. That’s an approach that’s really popular

sure that you have wafers that match really well in terms of the sort.
So sort good array here versus sort good array here.
If they match exactly — good die and bad die all match — I can get 100% yield
of that operation of the good dies. But the chances of that are very low.
There’s going to be some randomization of the two, and whatever that randomization is,
will be loss of good bonding to bad. Whereas with chip to wafer,
I can dictate the terms. I can singulate and have known good dies
that I’ve tested at the chip level, and then only bond known good to a known good base position.
